title: Environmental Regulations, Air and Water Pollution, and Infant Mortality in India
research_question: Do environmental regulations targeting air and water pollution in a developing country with weak regulatory institutions actually reduce ambient pollution concentrations, and do the resulting air quality improvements translate into measurable gains in infant health? Furthermore, why might regulations succeed in one pollution domain but fail in another within the same country?
data_description: The authors compiled a novel city-level panel dataset for India spanning 1986–2007. Air pollution data, drawn from the Central Pollution Control Board's National Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Programme, cover roughly 140 cities and 572 monitors measuring particulate matter (PM), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2). Water pollution data, from the National Water Monitoring Programme, cover 489 monitors in 424 cities along 162 rivers, measuring biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), dissolved oxygen (DO), and fecal coliforms. Regulation data on Supreme Court Action Plans, mandatory catalytic converter requirements, and the National River Conservation Plan were assembled from CPCB, Ministry of Environment and Forests, and SPCB sources. City-level annual infant mortality data come from Vital Statistics of India and state registrar offices. Supplementary data include district-level census demographics, consumption expenditures, Times of India pollution and corruption mentions, and Transparency International corruption measures.
institutional_context: India offers a setting with rapid economic growth, severe ambient pollution (the worst air pollution among 132 countries assessed), and regulatory institutions widely viewed as weak. Following the Water Act (1974), Air Act (1981), and the 1984 Bhopal disaster, India developed an extensive environmental regulatory apparatus involving the Central and State Pollution Control Boards and the Ministry of Environment and Forests. The paper focuses on three flagship policies adopted at staggered times across cities: Supreme Court Action Plans (beginning with Delhi in 1996, expanding to 17 cities by 2003) requiring suites of measures in critically polluted cities; mandatory catalytic converters on new petrol vehicles, imposed in four metros in 1995 and 45 additional cities in 1998; and the National River Conservation Plan, which since 1985 has financed sewage treatment infrastructure across 164 cities on 35 rivers. The Supreme Court played an unusually active enforcement role for air policies, while water policy implementation was fragmented across agencies.
